zones.label: Column 1

Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent scan reading; the returned transcription follows this copy, not a normalized headword list.

lines.note: Met. completes per met. from f342. Mutenna hito applies the unpointed-text image to a person who is not easily understood; the Portuguese en continues without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: tende, nem ſe ſabe declarar bem. ¶

lines.note: The person cannot make himself understood or explain himself well. Mu- begins a second example of the same adjectival expression.
Mutenna koto wo yuu or suru means saying or doing unintelligible things. The alternative verbs belong to the same example.

runs.text: zer couſas, que não ſe entendem.

lines.note: Zer completes fazer; the Portuguese defines the actions as things that cannot be understood. This closes the preceding page’s entry.
Mutǒ is explained by katana nashi, without a sword. Sẽ is an unexpanded abbreviation, and no punctuation is supplied after eſpada.
Mutǒ ni shite teki ni vǒ describes meeting an enemy without a sword. The printed vǒ is retained instead of modernizing the Japanese verb.
Catana occurs within the Portuguese translation. The next Japanese example repeats Mutǒni, whose damaged initial M was misrecognized as A.
Vǒ completes mutǒni mairi vǒ, glossed as encountering someone unarmed. The caron remains part of the printed verb form.
Mutoku is explained by toku nashi, without benefit or profit. The Portuguese offers two closely related constructions.
Receber proueito completes “without receiving benefit.” This short continuation belongs to mutoku, not to the next adverb.
Muttato is an adverb for inconsiderate or disorderly action. The scan retains the e in Inconſideradamente, which OCR omitted.

The gloss completes imperfectamente and adds “without order.” The low-register label B. is italic here: its narrow sloping capital matches italic Bicho, unlike the upright B of Bup. elsewhere on this page.
Musha is explained by takei mono and glossed as an armed soldier. The Japanese explanatory phrase remains separate from the Portuguese.
Mushaburi ga yoi describes a good soldierly appearance. A visible paragraph mark, omitted by OCR, introduces the example.
The gloss adds the bearing or manner of a soldier. This completes the illustration of mushaburi.
Muxabet is glossed as absence of difference. The final bare t is retained; it must not be expanded into an extra printed syllable.
Mushabugyǒ is an officer compared with a sergeant. The circumstantial description of commanding soldiers continues below.
The officer governs or directs the soldiers. This completes the military-office definition rather than introducing a new headword.
Mushabune is a vessel carrying soldiers. The visible x restores the headword from OCR Mu,abune.
Mushaburi refers the reader to Muxa, where the example concerning soldierly bearing occurs. Vide is italic, while the referenced Japanese word is upright.

runs.text: Certa laya de calçado de palha

lines.note: Mushawarangi names a kind of straw footwear. The historical warangi sequence is preserved rather than assimilated to a modern spelling.

runs.text: como alparcas de que vſão os ſoldados.

lines.note: The footwear is compared with alparcas worn by soldiers. The scan’s initial a corrects OCR olparcas.
Mushae is a picture of wars or battles. The final ye is the printed form for the picture-related element.
Muxe describes choking or something going down the wrong way. The Portuguese phrase has the visible separation no goto; the principal form ſuru remains literal.
The choking occurs while drinking wine or water. The scan reads agoa, not OCR agna; the small separator after vinho is retained as a period. Qe- begins kemuri.
Kemuri ni muſuru means choking on smoke. Preserve the example’s long ſ despite x in Muxe and muxete elsewhere in the entry.
Namida ni muxete is choking with tears. The Portuguese explains inability to speak and continues its divided verb below.
Lar completes falar, giving “unable to speak with tears.” This closes the crying example.
Muxebi has the same meaning and is said to occur in the same phrases. No additional principal forms are supplied beyond the printed u.

runs.text: Cozer algũa couſa com o ba-

lines.note: Muxi is steaming food rather than choking. The principal part uita is preserved as historical morphology, and ba- starts Portuguese bafo.
The cooking uses the vapour of hot water. Mangiǔ wo musu illustrates steaming buns; the historical g spelling is retained.

runs.text: Cozer desta maneira hũs pãosſinhos de trigo.

lines.note: The buns are described as small wheat breads cooked in this way. Hũs has a tilde over u; pãosſinhos retains the visible s/ſ sequence. Its n is heavily abraded and supplied from surviving lower strokes and the word’s context.
Muxi here means without a beginning, as Fajime naxi and Sẽ principio explain. Enlargement shows a word space before naxi.

runs.text: Couſa eterna, ſẽ principio nẽ fim.

lines.note: Muxi mujǒ is rendered as something eternal, without beginning or end. The printed mujǒ is retained rather than regularized to an expected modern expression.
A separate muxi entry means an insect or intestinal worms. The following example begins with the object muxi-.
Muxi wo vazzurǒ means suffering from worms. The printed vazzurǒ retains both z types and its caron.
Muxi ga vocoru describes an attack of worm-related illness. The initial v in vocoru is retained as printed.
The explanation adds stomach pain. Muxi ga xe- begins another expression, completed by qu on the following row.
Muxi ga xequ is marked X. for regional usage. The upright label is followed by Portuguese describing the worms pressing and tormenting someone.

runs.text: as lombrigas a alguem, ou dor de barriga, ou

lines.note: The Portuguese describes torment from worms or pain in the abdomen. The final ou introduces the alternative organ on the next row.
Eſtamago completes the reference to stomach pain. This short row remains part of the same explanatory example.
Muxibami describes an insect gnawing or eating something. The principal part ǒda is preserved rather than changed to a modern past ending.
Algũa couſa supplies the object of the insect’s eating. The preceding Japanese verb is therefore transitive in this gloss.

runs.text: Raſto, ou ſinal que deixa o bicho na

lines.note: Muxicui first denotes the trace or mark left by an insect. The material bearing the mark is specified below.

runs.text: madeira comida, ou notra couſa. ¶ Itẽ a meſ-

lines.note: The mark occurs in eaten wood or another object; notra is retained as printed. Itẽ then introduces the affected object itself as another sense.

runs.text: ma couſa como fruita, &c. comida do bicho.

lines.note: The second sense is the insect-eaten thing itself, such as fruit. This completes the distinction between damage marks and damaged material.
Muximochi here denotes a steamed preparation of Mochis. Mochis is a Japanese-derived word embedded in the Portuguese explanation, unlike the headword.

runs.text: com o bafo de agoa quente.

lines.note: The preparation is cooked with hot-water vapour. The m of com is heavily abraded; its surviving lower strokes and the phrase support com rather than OCR cou.

runs.text: Peßoa que tem lombrigas, ou dor

lines.note: This muximochi denotes a person with intestinal worms or abdominal pain, not the steamed food at the end of the other column.
De barriga completes the alternative symptom, abdominal pain. The short continuation closes this distinct muximochi entry.

runs.text: Certa laya de letria cozida com

lines.note: Muximugui is described as a kind of noodle-like preparation. Its method of cooking is specified on the next row.
The preparation is cooked with hot-water vapour. This completes the food definition and distinguishes it from the surrounding homophonous entries.
Muxin is explained by kokoro nashi and first glossed as inanimate. The Portuguese list of examples continues below.
The first sense is lacking sensation, as with trees and stones. A separate, previously omitted physical row introduces another sense immediately below.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Pejo, & repugnancia que hum de-

lines.note: This complete printed row was omitted by OCR. It introduces the shame or reluctance one ought to feel when making a request; de- joins uia below. Both text and a native-image crop are restored under a fresh ID.

runs.text: uia ter quando pede a alguem que dè, ou faça

lines.note: Uia completes deuia: the shame one should feel when asking someone to give or do something. This clause depends on the restored preceding row.
Muxin no shomǒ illustrates a request liable to impose on another person. De- begins the Portuguese desejo across the next line.

runs.text: ſejo, ou petição com que hum pode molestar a

lines.note: The wish or petition may trouble another person. This explains the social reluctance described in the restored row.
After completing “another,” the entry starts hito ni muxin or muxinna koto wo yuu, asking someone for something with reluctance.

runs.text: Dizer a alguem couſas que hũ

lines.note: The example means saying to someone things one is reluctant to say. Dizer a has a visible word boundary; the damaged final abbreviation is read as hũ, not OCR hoi.

runs.text: repugna, ou deuia de ter pejo por o não enfadar

lines.note: The speaker hesitates or ought to feel shame, so as not to annoy the other person. Pejo repeats the noun in the restored line, rather than OCR peyo.
Ou moleſtar completes the concern about troubling the person addressed. This closes the extended request-related sense of muxin.
Muxiqi is explained by iro nashi and glossed “without colour.” The Japanese explanatory phrase is not a Portuguese-embedded term.
Muxiqina is the adjective for something colourless. The gloss begins with a visibly lowercase c, retained rather than capitalized.
Muxiri means plucking. Tori wo mu- begins the first example, plucking a bird; the principal form itta is retained.
Tori wo muxiru is plucking a bird. Vata wo mu- then begins an example involving cotton or loose fibre.
Vata wo muxiru is teasing or separating fibre. The enlarged word has two r types in borra, though the preceding o is weak; kusa wo muxiru begins the next example.
Kusa wo muxiru is pulling herbs or grass; hana wo muxiru starts the corresponding example for a flower.

runs.text: Tirar com a mão as folhas da roſa, ou depinicar

lines.note: The flower example is explained as pulling the rose’s leaves or petals off by hand. The coordinated phrase continues below.
After completing the rose example, ke wo muxiru introduces pulling out hair. The large-tailed Q is ordinary printed letterform, not a new section initial.
Cabelos supplies the object of arrancar, completing the hair-plucking example. This is the final continuation of muxiri.
Muxiro is a mat. Muxiro wo utsu means making mats; the Portuguese Fa continues without a printed terminal hyphen.
Zer completes fazer, making mats. Muxiro wo shiku introduces spreading a mat, with Eſtẽ- beginning its translation.

The translation is spreading the mat on the floor. Enlargement shows faint upper and lower strokes of e between t and i in eſteira, followed by the separate no; muxiro ni tsuku begins the next example.
Muxiro ni tsuku is glossed as lying down in bed. The mat expression is interpreted through its use as bedding.
Muxiroxiqi is glossed as a mistress or concubine and described as little used. Palaura is one printed word, not OCR palaur a.
Muxit denotes a lie or false testimony. The final t is retained as a checked ending, without supplying a modern extra syllable.
Hito ni muxit wo iy kakuru means directing a false accusation at someone. In muxituo the object particle follows the printed final t.
Tar completes aleuantar: raising false testimony against someone. The Portuguese precisely explains the accusation sense of the example.

runs.text: Azia que ſe ſente na boca por cau-

lines.note: Muxizzu is described as an acid sensation in the mouth. The cause is explained in the continuation below.

runs.text: ſa do ruim eſtamago, ou comer indigesto.

lines.note: The sensation is attributed to an upset stomach or indigestible food. The historical eſtamago spelling is retained.
The printed example describes this acid sensation arising. Preserve Muxizzuqiga literally rather than deleting its qi to match a familiar modern expression; the paragraph mark is visible.

runs.text: ou vir à boca eſte azedume.

lines.note: The translation adds acid coming up into the mouth. The grave in à is a Portuguese accent, distinct from Japanese vowel-length marks.
Muxǒ is explained by shǒ nashi, lacking substance or vitality. The scan has Muxǒ, not Mixǒ, and the divided Portuguese word ends in -tan-, not -tar-.
Cia completes substancia, followed by vigour. Muxǒna hito begins an example applying this lack of animation to a person.

runs.text: mem que està fora de ſeu juizo, & ſentido por

lines.note: The person is outside his normal judgement or awareness. The word is ſeu, with long s, not OCR feu.
Illness or sleep supplies the cause. Muxǒni naru then illustrates entering such a state.

runs.text: Ficar fora de ſi, ou perder o juizo.

lines.note: The translation describes becoming beside oneself or losing judgement. It completes the state-change example rather than introducing another headword.
Muxo, without a printed long-vowel mark, denotes a grave or burial place. Its spelling is kept distinct from adjacent Muxǒ entries.
This Muxǒ means absence of obstruction, as sawari nashi explains. The Portuguese abbreviation is Sẽ, not Sè.
Muxǒ mugue means without impediment or hindrance. The mark over the first o is lightly printed and retained as the OCR-aligned caron.
Estoruo completes the no-hindrance gloss. The final S. is an upright written-language label.
Muxǒ muxi is glossed as neither being born nor dying and marked Bup. The printed nacer is preserved rather than modernized.
Muxoſa denotes idleness or doing nothing. Mu- begins the illustrative phrase continued on the next row.
Muxoſani shite iru means remaining idle. The translation’s final na- belongs to nada below.
Da completes nada and is the only running body text on this row. OCR’s attached Miuxi, was a duplicate misreading of the separately retained catchword Muxu., not a lost headword.
